lead.title: The Soothsayer: The Gators have all the motivation they need
lead.dek: Franz Beard: From Jadan Baugh’s shot at history to a Citrus Bowl push, the Soothsayer says the Gators have every reason to run over Florida State, plus his full SEC picks.
lead.author: Franz Beard
lead.html:
Photo: UAA

“When you’re up to your ass in alligators it’s difficult to remember that your original intention was to drain the swamp.” – Origin unknown.

The Florida State Seminoles can relate. Their athletic program is drowning in debt (pushing $500 million), they’d love to get out of the ACC (if they could afford it), they’re on the hook for $48.7 million to Mike Norvell of which half is due in a couple of weeks, and they’ve hired Glenn Schumann, the Georgia defensive coordinator to be their next head coach. Schumann, they think is a savior, but he comes with a price tag. He makes $2.2 million at Georgia and it’s probable the FSU contract will be close to triple that number. He will also need at least $30 million to make FSU’s roster competitive for next season.

The ever so sage Ivey Van Sickle once quipped about a 1970s version desperate financial situation, “To get out of a mess like this it’s going to take some folks with more money than they’ve got brains.” Indeed.

So, yes, Florida State has a swampful of alligators to deal with and we aren’t even talking about today’s football game (3:30 p.m., ABC) at The Big Bricked-Over Erector Set featuring the 20th-ranked Florida Gators (7-4, 5-4 SEC). Florida State is 5-6 against a slew of mediocre opponents from the ACC. Meanwhile the Florida Gators (7-4, 5-4 SEC) have three top 20 wins in Southeastern Conference play under their belts to go with the possibility of (1) a third straight win to end the regular season; (2) the first eight-win regular season since 2020; (3) a shot at playing in the Citrus Bowl; (4) a possible ninth win if they win their bowl game; and (5) adding Jadan Baugh’s name among the truly elite running backs in University of Florida history.

Three straight wins to end the year will take some of the sting that comes with going 3-4 in the middle of the season after a 4-0 start that put the Gators in the top ten and had pundits predicting a College Football Playoff season. Well, that didn’t happen but the Gators have rediscovered their lost mojo by whacking Kentucky in Lexington and Vanderbilt at home. The last time the Gators won eight games in the regular season was in the COVID season of 2020 when a Shoegate loss to LSU set off a three-loss ending.

A third straight win could be just what the Gators need to elbow their way past Oklahoma and Ole Miss into the Citrus Bowl where the opponent could be Ohio State. The Gators own a two-game win streak over the Buckeyes (2006 national championship game and 2011 Gator Bowl), whose head coach is former UF grad assistant Ryan Day. Perhaps a foretelling of things to come, but wins over FSU and whoever the Gators play in a bowl game would be No. 9 for Jon Sumrall. He won nine games in his first season as Tulane’s head coach, which set the stage for an American Conference championship and a College Football Playoff berth last year.

Finally, there is the incentive to unleash Jadan Baugh. A year ago, he had 904 yards entering the season finale with FSU. He carried the ball 38 times, gained 266 yards and scored two touchdowns, finishing the season with 1,170 yards and eight rushing touchdowns. This year he needs 20 against the Seminoles to become the first running back in Florida history to have back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons. That’s something neither Errict Rhett (4,163 career yards, 34 rushing touchdowns) nor Emmitt Smith (3,928 yards, 36 rushing touchdowns) ever accomplished. Baugh enters today’s game with 2,823 career yards and 31 rushing touchdowns. Baugh is 123 yards behind sixth place Tim Tebow on the Florida all-time rushing list. With a monstrous game (262 yards) against the Seminoles, he could surpass Fred Taylor for fifth.

While the Gators have plenty of incentives to run roughshod over the Seminoles, they have to be aware that this is an audition game for the entire FSU roster. The new coach will be watching, taking notes and likely starting a who stays and who goes list. The Seminoles are a middle of the pack ACC offensive team and bottom feeder when it comes to defense. They throw a lot of interceptions, have trouble protecting the passer and completing passes with any measure of consistency. They can’t get off the field on third down, rarely turn an opponent over and give up way too many rushing yards.

Still, FSU will be motivated and that makes the Seminoles a team the Gators can’t take lightly. The Soothsayer understands fully that the Seminoles have their backs to the wall, but believes Florida will have answers.

The Sayer Says Sooth!: The Gators have every reason to go ground and pound, not just because they want history for Jadan Baugh but because controlling the clock with the running game makes life easier for the defense. A monster game from Baugh is entirely possible and a sack-a-thon for the defense. The Gators are favored by 6.5 points. The Seminoles should be so lucky if the game is that close.

THE SEC SOOTHSAYER

FRIDAY GAMES

No. 3 Texas (9-2, 6-2 SEC) at Texas A&M (4-7, 1-7 SEC), 7:30 p.m., ABC: Texas has the advantage of playing on Friday. If the Longhorns beat their country cousins in College Station it puts all the pressure on Alabama. If Bama wins it doesn’t matter what Texas or Tennessee do, so first and foremost, the Longhorns have to take care of business against the Aggies. Texas is an 11.5-point favorite largely because its defense is good enough to overcome Arch Manning’s brain dead moments. The Aggies won’t go bowling and will go down as college football’s most disappointing team in 2026 if they go down in flames for a fifth straight game. It will be Senior Day in Aggieland. The roar from the crowd when Marcel Reed is introduced will be of the thank God he’s gone type. The Sayer Says Sooth!: Texas has won five straight games, cooling the talk about Steve Sarkisian needing to find another place to be gainfully employed. Of course, lose to the Aggies and the Fire Sark talk heats up again. It’s not going to happen. Will Muschamp’s defense will rule the day and the Longhorns get to thumb their snooty noses at their Aggie cousins.

Mississippi State (5-6, 2-6 SEC) at No. 22 Ole Miss (7-4, 4-4 SEC), 12 noon, ABC: Ole Miss is an 18.5-point favorite to give Trinidad Chambliss a dandy senior day sendoff. Despite all its injuries, Ole Miss still has better players than Mississippi State, whose own injury woes have been devastating. Mississippi State with Kamario Taylor healthy and Fluff Bothwell at 100 percent is dangerous. With Taylor done for the year and Bothwell a shell of what he was before his injury in game five, Mississippi State has still put up a good fight, enough that with a break or two the Bulldogs could already be bowl eligible. That is their motivation today, but it won’t be enough. The Sayer Says Sooth!: A big numbers day for Trinidad and a taste of next year in the second half when Deuce Knight gets to show off his QB skills. It shouldn’t be close and won’t be unless Ole Miss decided to mail it in.

SATURDAY GAMES

Georgia Tech (3-8) at No. 1 Georgia (10-1, 8-1 SEC), 3:30 p.m., ABC: Georgia is going to win this game. The only question for the Bulldogs is by how much. It’s a chance to make a Heisman statement for Gunner Stockton, who has this game and the SEC Championship Game to make a last ditch pitch to win the big trophy. For Georgia Tech, it’s about keeping it close. A blowout loss and head coach Brent Key could be sent packing. The Sayer Says Sooth!: Gunner Stockton, Heisman Trophy QB. Now who in their right mind would have thought that possible, but because the Bulldogs are so dominant he’s seriously in the running. Georgia is a 35.5-point favorite. Why is the spread that close?

No. 5 Tennessee (9-2, 6-2 SEC) at Vanderbilt (4-7, 1-7 SEC), 7 p.m., ESPN: The Vols have quarterback issues and DeSean Bishop may not play. With their defense, they probably need only bare minimum contributions from the offense. If Texas loses to the Aggies and the Vols beat Vandy, they not only make the SEC Championship Game for a shot at Georgia, but they probably move into the top four in the College Football Playoff poll. Vandy can make it close for awhile, but that Tennessee front four will dominate in the fourth quarter. The Sayer Says Sooth!: The Vols are favored by 13.5 points. While making the SEC Championship Game offers plenty of incentive, UT is in very good shape to get a first round bye in the event Texas beats the Aggies and then loses to Georgia in Atlanta. Vandy will put up a fight for awhile, then fall apart late.

Auburn (7-4, 4-4 SEC) at No. 6 Alabama (9-2, 6-2 SEC), 7:30 p.m., ABC: Alabama can make the SEC Championship Game with a win even if Texas and Tennessee win their games. But what happens if the unthinkable takes place in Tuscaloosa? A third loss in the regular season would also be No. 11 in Kalen DeBoer’s three years on the job. Even with six losses his first year at Alabama in 2007, Nick Saban never lost 11 games in three years. Bama fans remember stuff like this. Even worse, the Bama boosters who write the big checks think about things like this. Don’t think for a second Kalen DeBoer isn’t sitting on a very hot seat. Auburn has beaten Georgia in Athens. Beat Bama in Tuscaloosa? It could happen if Byrum Brown picks up big yards on the ground and remembers to throw the ball to people wearing the same color shirt he’s wearing. The Sayer Says Sooth!: The oddsmakers in Las Vegas have established Alabama as a 15.5-point favorite. That’s what it should be, but strange things happen in the Iron Bowl. The Soothsayer like Alabama in a chest clutcher.

No. 17 Oklahoma (7-4, 5-3 SEC) at No. 23 Missouri (7-4, 4-4 SEC), 4:15 p.m., SEC Network: Missouri’s offense has been average at best against really good defenses and Oklahoma’s is one of the best in the country, particularly because interim offensive coordinator Jason Whitten has the Sooners controlling the clock while limiting the time the defense has to be on the field. If Whitten can dial up another ball control game and John Mateer can avoid turnovers, Oklahoma can win this game. Missouri’s hope to win requires its defense to force a bunch of four-and-outs and keep Austin Simmons upright. If Simmons has time to throw, Mizzou’s got a chance. The Sayer Says Sooth!: Since Whitten started calling the plays, the Sooners are 3-0 and they’ve moved up to No. 3 in the SEC in time of possession. Missouri struggles on getting off the field on third down. If the Tigers can’t get stops, they’ll lose this one. The Soothsayer sees Oklahoma in a white knuckles win that takes the interim label off Whitten and secures Venables place as the Boomer Sooner honcho next year.

No. 19 Louisville (8-3) at Kentucky (7-4, 5-4 SEC), 12 noon, ESPN2: Ever since the Wildcats cracked the top 10 they’ve been backsliding, losing three in a row. They’re going against a Louisville team that (a) runs the football and (b) doesn’t turn the ball over, which is why the Cardinals are 3-point favorites to win in Lexington. For the Wildcats to win the game, they’ve got to stuff the Louisville run and get more productivity – one TD and three picks in the last three games – from QB Kenny Minchey. A win and the Wildcats probably return to their traditional winter home, also known as the Music City Bowl. Lose and they go to the Birmingham Bowl where if they lose they are required to stay another week as punishment. The Sayer Says Sooth: It’s an ACC vs. SEC battle. Even if UK has lost three in a row, the Cats are SEC, therefore the Sooth Sayer likes them to win.

LSU (6-5, 3-5 SEC) at Arkansas (4-7, 2-6 SEC), 12:45 p.m., SEC Network: If the Lane Train ends its three-game losing skid with a win in Fayette Nam, it will bring the per win cost down to somewhere around $20 million. LSU spent more than $55 million firing Brian Kelly and his staff, then hired Lane for $13 mill a year and a new staff for a cool $10 or so. Then came NIL, the portal and another cash outlay of somewhere in the neighborhood of $50 million. With a win against Arkansas, they can bring the cost per win down to a “more manageable” $18 million. That’s progress for you. The Sayer Says Sooth!: As if LSU hasn’t enough troubles with the SEC poised to vote the Tigers off the island on Wednesday of next week, they’ve got to worry that the Tigers might mail it in against Arkansas. If it’s close or an upset then it is clear Lane lost the locker room. The pressure is clearly on LSU, but the Tigers should win, maybe by less than the 14.5-point spread.

South Carolina (6-5, 4-5 SEC) at Clemson (7-4), 3 p.m., ESPN2: If LaNorris Sellers not only plays but is able to function at a higher capacity than he did last week against Georgia, the Gamecocks will walk away with a win over the Fighting Dabos. If he’s unable to take off running when the pocket collapses, the Gamecocks are in deepest and darkest. Worse yet, if his ankle gets dinged again and he leaves the game, Clemson probably wins the game. South Carolina is favored by six. The Sayer Says Sooth!: For Clemson this game is an audition. In the event LSU gets booted from the SEC, Clemson has the kind of top to bottom athletic program, history of national championships in football and a true SEC atmosphere at Death Valley, unlike those at Miami or North Carolina. The Tigers need this win desperately but so do the Gamecocks, who have lost by 28 points in each of their last two games. It’s a tale of two coaches who are trying to impress boosters who think it’s time for a change. Make this one a tight sphincter win for Shane Beamer over Dabo Swinney.

items.title: Will Heartburn Over the Seminoles Ruin Our Turkey and Dressing?
items.dek: Every Thanksgiving table has a fourth-and-goal moment. Florida’s football season is that sliver of pie, and Buddy Martin is reaching for the fork Friday in Tallahassee.
items.author: Buddy Martin
items.html:
Will Seminoles Experience a “Croak at Doak?”

Every Thanksgiving table has a fourth-and-goal moment. The turkey has been carved and the stuffing has been audibled into a second helping.

Then the sweet potato pie sits alone on the platter with one sliver left, and everybody has seen it.

You have two plays. You can announce, “Anybody want that last piece?” That’s the coward’s play-action. It invites Aunt Edna to blitz off the edge with “Oh no, you go ahead,” while she tracks your fork like a safety reading the quarterback’s eyes.

Or you can run out the clock. You study the ceiling and discuss the Lions game. You ask for the cranberry sauce you’ve never wanted in your life. Meanwhile every fork at the table is in a three-point stance.

Then there’s the physics. It might be the one bite too many, the extra yard that turns a fine meal into a belt-loosening, recliner-bound, call-the-cardiologist situation. Or it might be the game-winning field goal of the whole feast.

Nobody knows until the fork leaves the sideline. How much is enough, and how much is too much to expect?

Florida’s football season is that sliver of pie.

Back in the summer, my podcast pals were asked to commit to a win total. The line was 7.5. Everybody else rushed to eight like a free safety on a flea-flicker. I stared at that number the way you stare at the last piece of pie, looking and looking and looking, trying to find a way to digest it.

For the life of me, I couldn’t find where the other half a win was coming from. You can’t win half a game, and I couldn’t find a whole one either. I was the lone holdout on the committee, which is a nice way of saying I was the guy punting on fourth-and-one.

I won’t lie and claim I called every loss and every win. After four losses in five tries, it didn’t seem to matter. Then it suddenly did, after two straight wins.

Funny how a little gravy changes the mood of the whole huddle.

Heartburn in Tallahassee

So here we are. The No. 20 Gators are 7-4 and favored by about a touchdown Friday in Tallahassee. Win, and it’s No. 8, the number everybody circled in July while I sat there like the guy who brings a casserole to a tailgate.

Will heartburn over the Seminoles ruin our turkey and dressing? Only if you let a 5-6 team with a bowl bid on the line crash the table like an uninvited cousin who eats your leftovers and critiques the gravy.

But look at that kitchen. Mike Norvell was fired Nov. 1 with a buyout of roughly $50 million, which is a lot of money to pay a man to stop coaching.

The scouting director has been running the team since. Promoting from the film room is how you know the grease fire has already started.

Make hay while the cook’s away

Florida State hired Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann on Monday, but he’s expected to stay in Athens through the playoff. So Friday the Seminoles get an interim coach, a lame-duck game plan and a fan base already scrolling real estate listings for the next guy.

That’s the window. Once Schumann shows up with a fresh staff and a portal budget, this game gets harder to win. Eat the pie while the cook is at another table.

What’s on the plate

Eight wins is the slice everybody wants. Nine is the whole second pie, and it would be Florida’s first nine-win season since 2019. That would take a win Friday and another in a bowl game. I’m not greedy. I’m a man who studies the sliver, not the whole platter.

The verdict

Maybe on Thanksgiving we should just be grateful for food on the table and a program that appears to have been turned around.

But Friday afternoon in Tallahassee, I won’t wait for anybody to say “go ahead.” I’ll say, “I’ve got it,” and reach for the fork. If it’s one bite too many, so be it. I’d rather be a little too full than sit there wondering.

Please pass the whipped cream.

items.title: Pregame Analysis: No. 20 Florida Gators (7-4, 5-4) vs. Florida State Seminoles (5-6, 3-5)
items.dek: Despite the Seminoles’ coaching transition, there is always something to play for in the Sunshine Showdown. Loren Meadows breaks down the matchups and predicts Florida 28, FSU 17.
items.author: Loren Meadows
items.html:
Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media

Despite the Seminoles transition there is always something to play for in the Sunshine Showdown.

By Loren Meadows, GatorBaitMedia.com Football Analyst, Host of The Gator Lowdown with Loren Meadows

Jon Sumrall takes his team into Doak Campbell Stadium for his first taste of one of the country’s most popular rivalries. The players grew up together, the fans work together, some even live under the same roof. While the programs seem to be in different spaces right now. Florida is looking to stamp the year with three straight wins while an upset will give FSU its 6th win and a bowl trip for interim coach and FSU alum Rick Stockstill. Rivalries matter and losses in these games have consequences. Both teams know that, and there will be no love letter exchanged in Tallahassee this weekend.

Florida State Offense

Key Players: QB #14 Ashton Daniels (6-2, 225, 5th Yr./Auburn), #8 WR Micahi Danzy (6-1, 194, Jr.), #21 RB Zay Parks (5-11, 204, Jr.)

Matchups To Watch: Ashton Daniels v. Florida’s Pass Rush, FSU Turnovers v. Explosive plays

Quarterback Ashton Daniels has been up and down all season and things have not been easy as the season has progressed as the injury bug has affected his weapons. Wide receiver Duce Robinson is out for the season. UF's Nov. 26 availability report lists running backs Ousmane Kromah and Amari Thomas out, with Quintrevion Wisner and Sam Singleton Jr. questionable. Those injuries have put pressure on Daniels to do more with his legs the past few weeks while trying to maintain some level of efficiency through the air. Daniels is completing just under 60 percent of his passes with 14 touchdowns and 14 interceptions. He has been better on the ground with 13 touchdowns and with 625 yards gained before inflation(sacks). Florida has struggled at times with mobile quarterbacks so look for FSU to get Daniels going early on the ground with the injuries on offense.

Despite the injuries in the backfield former walk on Zay Parks has taken on the role of the primary back to end the season. Despite his walk on status he appeared in nine games in 2025 and has appeared in all 11 games this season. Parks however had a rough go of it last week against NC State and he will be looking for an opportunity to break off some chunk runs against Florida.

On the perimeter FSU will be without Duce Robinson who tore his ACL on October 31 against Clemson. That has left Tallahassee native Micahi Danzy to shoulder the load as Daniels’ primary target. Danzy has size and speed and last season caught 4 passes for 49 yards and touchdown in the game in Gainesville. Look for FSU to move him around to create matchups in space that have troubled Florida at times.

Florida State Defense

Key Players: #10 LB Chris Jones (6-1, 231, Jr./Southern Miss), 11 DB CJ Richard Jr. (6-1, 200, Jr./Illinois State), #7 DB Ashlynd Barker (6-3, 217, 5th Yr.) #15 DL Rylan Kennedy (6-3, 251, Sr. Texas A&M)

Matchups To Watch: Florida Offensive Line v. FSU Defensive Line, Aaron Philo Legs v. FSU Secondary

As on offense FSU is dealing with injuries on defense including several defensive linemen. This will not be good as Florida will look to establish the run early to set the tone in the game as well as look to get Jadan Baugh his second straight 1,000-yard season. FSU will lean on a defense that is currently 15th in the ACC and surrendering 171 yards against the run and 237 per game through the air. A pair of transfers have emerged as the statistical leaders on the defense and a statement game against their most hated rival may make the change in location worth it. Southern Miss transfer Chris Jones leads the team in tackles 85 tackles, five for loss and six QB hurries. Illinois State transfer CJ Richard junior has followed up a successful 2025 with the FCS runner-up to solid transition to big boy football with 72 tackles. With Florida off and on up front there could be some cause and effect between Jones pressure of Philo and Richard finding the ball and creating turnovers.

Along with Richard, Ashlynd Barker has been solid after starting nine games a year ago. He is third on the team in tackles and tied for the lead in interceptions. The play action game will be key for Florida and Barker’s presence and ability to make plays will need to be on point if FSU is going to pull off the upset.

While the defensive line is banged up Texas A&M transfer Rylan Kennedy, listed questionable in UF's Nov. 26 report, had flourished in an expanded role at FSU. The first-year starter leads the team in sacks (6) and tackles for loss (9.5), and while the Florida offensive line has been a sore spot for most of the season Kennedy could present problems for a unit that had to make a midgame swap at center two weeks ago.

This game has always been about the line of scrimmage. The last two season Florida has dominated that matchup and it has resulted in solid wins in both games. Philo has added more to the running game and that should open enough room for Baugh and Duke Clark to get enough going to keep FSU at bay.

The Skinny: This weekend is about the rest of your life. Reunions, documentaries, trash talk among future teammates all rest on the results of weekends like these. Throw out the records, these teams have no love for one another. No one in Gainesville is feeling sorry for FSU nor do they care that they hired Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann to replace Mike Norvell earlier this week. What they do care about is that Jon Sumrall and his team have a chance to flip last year’s 4-8 record, beat the hated Seminoles for a third straight year and go to a bowl that takes place after Santa Claus comes to town. All accomplishments that should be celebrated as the program has already posted three Top 15 wins this season. Philo has been more effective with his legs than his arm the last two weeks and FSU will certainly sell out to stop Baugh from getting loose. There will have to be some moments where Florida wins on the perimeter and the Florida pass catchers have been effective enough at times to win when it matters. The defense has been up and down nearly every quarter if every game this season but have found the confidence to step up when the game is in the balance. Florida will get it done in an up and down game, but when it’s your rival a win is all that matters. Jon Sumrall goes 1-0 in the Sunshine Showdown.

Prediction: Florida 28 FSU 17

items.html:
Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media

It is game day in Tallahassee. No. 20 Florida closes the regular season this afternoon against Florida State at Doak Campbell Stadium, in front of a sellout crowd and a national television audience. Here is everything you need to know before kickoff.

Game information

Matchup: No. 20 Florida (7-4, 5-4 SEC) at Florida State (5-6, 3-5 ACC)

Kickoff: 3:30 p.m. ET today, Friday, Nov. 27, 2026

Site: Doak Campbell Stadium (Bobby Bowden Field), Tallahassee. The game is sold out.

TV: ABC. Tom Hart has the play-by-play, Roddy Jones is the analyst and Quint Kessenich reports from the sideline.

Streaming: ESPN app, ESPN+ and Fubo.

Series history

Florida leads the series 39-28-2 and has won the last two meetings. The Gators won 40-21 at The Swamp last season, when Jadan Baugh carried 38 times for 266 yards and three touchdowns.

Odds

Florida is a 6.5-point favorite, according to BetMGM. The total is 53.5. On the moneyline, Florida is minus-235 and Florida State is plus-190.

Weather

It will be a clear, cool afternoon in Tallahassee. The high is 59 degrees, temperatures will fall toward 39 by the end of the game, and the chance of rain is about 1 percent.

What to watch

Baugh and the number 20. Baugh has 980 rushing yards this season and needs 20 more to become the first player in Florida history with back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons. He has 16 rushing touchdowns. A year after his breakout game against the Seminoles in Gainesville, he can make history against them again, this time in Tallahassee.

Philo's run. Quarterback Aaron Philo has won his last two starts. He has passed for 1,727 yards and nine touchdowns this season, with 280 rushing yards and six rushing touchdowns.

A shorthanded Florida State. The Seminoles must win to reach bowl eligibility and avoid a third straight losing season, and they have to do it with a depleted roster under interim head coach Rick Stockstill. Mike Norvell was fired on Nov. 2, and Glenn Schumann takes over the program after the season. Schumann is not coaching today. Florida State is without top running backs Ousmane Kromah and Amari Thomas, both out for the season, leading receiver Duce Robinson, who is out with a knee injury, and both starting cornerbacks. Fourteen Seminoles missed last week's game. Quarterback Ashton Daniels has passed for 2,515 yards and 14 touchdowns and run for 459 yards and 13 touchdowns, but his 14 interceptions are the most in the FBS.

The stakes. Florida is already bowl-eligible. A win gives the Gators eight regular-season wins for the first time since 2020 and a third straight win in the series.

items.title: A time to give thanks and a Florida-FSU memory
items.dek: On Thanksgiving eve, Franz Beard remembers a Cambodian refugee family's gratitude, a lifetime of Gator memories, and the 2005 Florida-FSU week when Urban and Shelley Meyer called his mother in the hospital.
items.author: Franz Beard
items.html:
File photo: Florida linebacker Myles Graham celebrates with teammates during the Gators' 34-27 win over Vanderbilt at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.

On this quiet Thanksgiving eve, sitting at a 150-year old antique desk that belonged to my grandfather, the only sounds that pierce my dimly lit Lake Eustis condo are occasional chirps from my cockatiels Fred and Ethel and shifts in the wind outside that blow causing the rain to pelt the sliding glass door that leads to my patio.

The near silence is appreciated as I unclutter my mind, erasing the trivia of the day, replacing it with thoughts of loved ones who won’t be here to share Thanksgiving with me. Ever since early morning the video reel in my head has been replaying over and over again a Sunday morning from more than 45 years ago when I drove a family of Cambodian refugees from their government assisted apartment on Northeast 15th Avenue in Gainesville to First Baptist Church. They had escaped the killing fields of the dictator Pol Pot, crossing the border into Thailand where they spent more than two years in a refugee camp before they were sponsored to the United States.

From a purely cultural standpoint, Gainesville could have been Mars. Their three kids picked up English in a hurry and wondered out loud why mom and dad struggled with the language. School was across the street. Mom got a job cleaning at the school. Dad, a former lawyer in Cambodia, took part-time work while learning air conditioning repair out at Santa Fe. They had no car so they rode the bus everywhere they went although once a week they got rides up to the Winn-Dixie at the corner of 23rd and Main where they shopped with food stamps for bargains.

On the way to First Baptist Church, where they were members of a growing Sunday School class of internationals taught by Carleta and Dom Underwood, my mother and stepfather, I asked if they were adjusting to life in Gainesville. They smiled and with happy tears turning into rivers that streaked down their faces, their reply was something I have never forgotten.

In broken English she said, “We live in America where we are safe. We escaped or else we would be dead like most of our family.”

They had lived a good life in Cambodia. He was an important lawyer but when Pol Pot came to power they were enemies of the state. Their escape to the border was a harrowing experience but somehow they made it to Thailand and by God’s grace were sponsored to Gainesville where their Cambodian abundance was exchanged for a poverty-level existence in a strange new country.

There was no bitterness as they told me of their escape, live in the camps and the new life in America.

“Our children come home from school and they tell us we are so poor,” the husband said, struggling to find the right English words. “We tell our children that is not true. We have so much. We live in America. We have food, a home and we are safe and alive. We tell them one day if they study and learn they will be able to go to this great University of Florida. No, we are not poor. We have so much to be thankful for.”

All day long, I’ve been remembering those words. Comparatively speaking, my difficulties pale in comparison to that Cambodian family of five, but I remember the smiles on their faces, the feeling that only freedom can give you and the hope that the new life will surpass their most ambitious dreams.

That 10-minute drive to First Baptist Church that day left an indelible impression that the older I get, the more I appreciate the life I have been blessed to have. I’ve been to the mountaintop, all the way down to rock bottom and everything in between. I’ve gone to the places and done the things that first came alive in the National Geographic magazine collection of my fifth grade teacher at Lake Mary Elementary, Miss Tillis. I’ve been to 62 countries so far and there is still so much to see.

I started writing for the McComb Enterprise-Journal when I was 13 years old during my family’s three-year exile to Mississippi, a place where I made dear friends who remain my friends even today. I’ve had the chance to write extensively about the only team that ever really mattered to me, the Florida Gators. I loved the Baltimore Orioles and the Baltimore Colts, but Brooks Robinson and Jim Palmer retired from the Orioles, and before he traded Johnny Unitas to the San Diego Chargers, Jim Irsay moved the Colts to Indianapolis. Players and coaches come and go at Florida, but my bond with the Gators is unbreakable dating back to my first football game: Florida 18, Georgia Tech 17 in 1960.

I’ve been fortunate to go places and do things that I only dreamed to do when I was a kid. As a sports writer, I’ve been blessed to cover heavyweight championship fights, World Series, Super Bowls, the Masters and so many more games and events, but the games that mean the most and I carry with me everywhere I go are those which involved the Gators.

Thanksgiving has provided memories of Florida-Florida State games, one especially that stands out that I would like to share.

It was Florida State week in 2005, Urban Meyer’s first year as the Florida head coach. My mom was in ORMC in Orlando, struggling to stay alive after a surgeon had nicked her spinal cord. I was commuting back and forth from Gainesville to Orlando on a daily basis. On Tuesday after practice, Meyer tugged on my elbow, offered words of encouragement then asked if there was anything he and Shelley could do to help. My mother grew up three blocks from the UF campus. Her dad’s cousin was Dale Van Sickel, Florida’s first All-American. My mom’s love of the Gators knew no boundaries, but she was particularly fond of Urban and Shelley.

I thanked Urban for his concern and mentioned that my mother’s birthday was Sunday, the day after the FSU game. He asked if it would be okay to call her Thanksgiving morning. Of course I agreed.

Thanksgiving morning, with family filling the room at ORMC, the call came in from Urban and Shelley. It was more than a hi and howdy call. My mom’s physical and emotional demeanor changed on the spot. Before the call ended, Urban told my mom, “I understand you have a birthday coming up. What would you like for a birthday present?”

My mom replied, “Well, you could kick FSU’s butt!” to which Urban answered, “We’ll just have to make that birthday wish come true.”

If you were around at the time, you know what happened Saturday. Marcus Thomas blocked an FSU field goal that Reggie Lewis ran back for a touchdown. The late Avery Atkins, a true freshman starting because Vernell Brown was recovering from a broken ankle, shut down FSU’s 6-6 wide receiver Greg Carr, picking off a fourth quarter pass that sealed the win as well as recovering a fumble. Jarvis Herring also intercepted FSU QB Drew Weatherford and the defense sacked Weatherford five times. Chris Leak threw touchdown passes to Chad Jackson and Dallas Baker, Markus Manson ran for a TD and Chris Hetland kicked two field goals.

Final score Florida 34, FSU 7.

On his way back to the locker room after his post game press conference, Meyer whacked me on the butt with his Gatorade bottle and said, “That was for your mom. Happy birthday from Shelley, me and the Florida Gators.”

In the weeks prior to Thanksgiving and the football game, my mom had nearly died three times, but Sunday she was smiling, happy and telling anyone and everyone who would listen that Urban Meyer had personally called and told her that the Gators had made her birthday wish come true. Only a few days before we thought we had lost her.

My mom lived another 21 years. She breathed her last December 8, 2025, 97 years and 11 days from the day she arrived. In the span of those years, she was a constant inspiration and helper to so many just like that Cambodian family years before. She never saw color or circumstance, she only saw people who deserved to be loved. Her lasting legacy is the number of lives that were changed for the better by her love and care.

Today is my first Thanksgiving without my mother’s presence. Friday would have been her 98th birthday. I know exactly what she would tell me if she were still alive: “We are Gators and we never get tired of beating our country cousins from Tallahassee.”

Miss you Mom.

Published Nov. 24, 2026. Statistical update, Nov. 27: Florida lists Jadan Baugh at 980 rushing yards, 20 short of 1,000. Coaching references reflect the original publication date; Rick Stockstill is Florida State’s interim coach for today’s game.

Florida and Vanderbilt players on Nov. 21 at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium. Florida plays at Florida State on Friday. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.

A few thoughts to jump start your Tuesday morning:

Don’t even think about writing off Friday’s day-after-Thanksgiving renewal of the Florida-Florida State football rivalry (3:30 p.m., ABC) as just another game. This is the first Florida-FSU experience for Florida coach Jon Sumrall, but he is keenly aware of how this game’s importance has a ripple effect through the entire program as well as both state and national perceptions.

On paper, this game doesn’t carry the same national championship implications it had in the 1990s when both the Gators and Seminoles were fixtures in the race for the BCS title game. The Gators (7-4) need a win to enhance their chances of playing in either the Citrus Bowl in Orlando or the ReliaQuest Bowl in Tampa. For FSU (5-6) it’s a chance to avoid a third straight losing season while becoming bowl eligible. This does not include traditions, bragging rights and momentum that carries over to the recruiting trail.

“Anybody that says just another game, I don’t buy into that,” Sumrall said at his Monday press conference. “It’s not just another game – it’s an in-state rivalry. Those are different, but the world we live in are all big because we play in the SEC, and week in, week out, they’re all big games and they’re all challenging games. This is one that means something to so many people because the in-state rivalry component it is a bragging rights in-state game, which does matter.”

Not only bragging rights, but at stake for the 20th-ranked Gators (7-4) is a season-ending three-game winning streak which could give Florida its first eight-win regular season since Dan Mullen’s 2020 team. Eight wins in the regular season would exceed preseason expectations from the national news media, many of whom predicted a 6-6 season for the Gators against one of the nation’s tougher schedules.

Sumrall knows the value of eight wins, but from his perspective eight wins is a building block for the future.

“It’s better than six, it’s not as good as eight or nine or whatever,” Sumrall said. “I’m so micro right now at the moment. I want to win every game we play. I also haven’t shied away from the fact that I think as we’re growing as a program, we’re trying to build the foundation. We can’t shy away from milestones that show growth, and that may mean the first winning conference record in several years since 2020. That’s a big deal. Now, in order for us to go where we want to go long term, that’s not the end goal but there’s been some growth.

“I think trailing it at halftime the last several games and seeing a different mindset maybe to the first couple and how we’ve responded at times has been growth. But I’m glad that there’s a lot of things that we’ve accomplished. We’ve missed a lot of opportunities as well. I probably am such a realist that I don’t really feel real excited about winning seven games. I also understand the good of that too, but I’m not like man, we’ve accomplished so much. I feel a little bit frustrated by some of the missed opportunities we’ve had, but we will get there. There’s been growth in this football team. It hasn’t maybe been as fast as I wanted at times, but there has been growth, and we still have areas where we have to grow a lot to get to where we want to go long term here.”

The obvious place where growth has been slower than what is needed is the offensive line. In getting off to a 4-0 start, the O-line seemed like the least of Sumrall’s problems, but ever since game five inconsistency has reared a very ugly head. The Gators averaged nearly 500 yards per game and scored at least 50 points three times in September. Since then the Gators have struggled to score and have only had one game (Vanderbilt) in which they gained at least 400 yards.

The lack of consistency by the O-line has shown itself in the diminished rushing numbers for Jadan Baugh and the dip in passing yardage. Baugh, who needs 19 yards against Florida State to become Florida’s 1,000-yard rusher in back-to-back seasons, had 600 yards and 11 touchdowns in the first four games. In the seven games since he had just 380 yards and five touchdowns.

The Gators threw for 241 yards in the win over Vanderbilt, the first time since South Carolina in game six that was accomplished. Neither Aaron Philo nor Tramell Jones Jr. has thrown a touchdown pass to a wide receiver since Philo and Bailey Stockton connected in the South Carolina game.

The offensive line has to bear responsibility for the offensive slowdown.

“It’s the offensive line’s job to make sure the running back gets back to line of scrimmage, and it’s the running back job to do something from there,” Sumrall said. “We have at times not done a good enough job of getting the ball carrier back to line. That pisses me off. That drives me nuts. And then in protection, same deal. We’ve had times this year we’ve protected the passer well, and then we’ve had some really major missed opportunities to get the ball down the field because we didn’t have enough time in the pocket and so there’s been some good moments.

“There’s been some bad moments, more bad moments than I would like. I think it’s a frustrating deal because the offensive line, those guys care. Phil Trautwein cares, deeply. He’s passionate to get this right. Everybody on our offensive staff does. And I’ve said this before: the offensive line is the one position that needs nobody’s help to do their job well. It’s also the one position that everybody needs them to do well to do so that they can do their job. So the quarterback, the running backs, the receivers they all need the O-line to play well. The O-line needs nobody to play well, for them to play well.”

TO KICK OR NOT TO KICK, THAT IS THE QUESTION

A meeting of the presidents and chancellors of the Southeastern Conference’s 16 member schools has been called for December 3, the singular topic of discussion LSU’s future in the league. This is not one of those silly my bad, don’t do it again meetings more than make the people in charge feel they’ve been big meanies. This is the serious business of deciding if LSU deserves to continue as a member of the best and most prestigious athletic conference in the country.

At the heart of the matter is LSU’s continued defiance of the SEC and whether or not the SEC has the right to sanction any school that refuses to abide by its rules. This feud began back in the summer when LSU football coach Lane Kiffin attempted to add players who were already in NFL training camps to his fall roster. Kiffin backed down eventually, but basketball coach Will Wade, already no stranger to controversy, elected to pick up the torch and run with it. Kiffin never added the NFL players to his roster, but Wade not only added to his roster RJ Luis, two years removed from college basketball and a veteran of the G-League, but actually played him in a game.

LSU president Wade Rousse ordered Wade to remove Luis from the roster the next day, but it seems that gesture is a day too late in the minds of the other league leaders. They have the votes to expel LSU if that’s what they choose to do. The question is do they kick the Tigers to the curb or do they sanction some or all of the LSU athletic teams?

Some talking heads say the SEC would never go so far as to remove LSU, but if that’s not a distinct possibility, then why hold a conclave in which expulsion is the only topic of discussion? Voting LSU off the island is a very real possibility.

And, it has to be done quickly because once the Protect College Sports legislation passes and becomes law, there will be a moratorium on schools in the power conferences hopscotching from one conference to another. The open window to fire LSU and hire someone new is for a short time only so things will happen in a hurry.

The question of who would the SEC go after to replace LSU might be the card that keeps LSU in the SEC. The most logical candidates would be Florida State, Miami, Clemson, North Carolina, Oklahoma State and Kansas.

Of that group, Miami, North Carolina and Kansas have the most to offer. FSU would swim through a sewer to join the SEC, but it’s drowning in debt and doesn’t offer any real increase in the SEC footprint. Miami, with its beaches and night life, has the appeal of Nashville and is the eighth-largest TV market in the country. North Carolina adds the Charlotte, Raleigh and Greensboro TV markets plus a state that ranks ninth nationally in population. The only problem for North Carolina would be what happens to sports such as men’s soccer, men’s lacrosse, wrestling, fencing and field hockey. The Tar Heels regularly win national championships in those sports but they aren’t sponsored by the SEC.

Kansas basketball brings serious appeal. Kansas basketball is off the charts in TV viewership and along with Kentucky is the winningest program in college basketball history. Its proximity to Missouri, Oklahoma and Arkansas plus its former Big 12 relationships with both Texas and Texas A&M adds to the appeal.

But whatever happens, the SEC has to move quickly. The votes may be there to expel LSU but is that what is best for the SEC?

ONE FINAL PITHY THOUGHT: Florida-Florida State week makes me think fondly of Bill Peterson. Yeah, I know. He was the coach at FSU and I’m a Gator lifer with the family name (Van Sickel) on a plaque on the Ben Hill Griffin Stadium wall, but Pete made football fun and entertaining. And don’t get me started on some of his “Pete-isms” like the one at Cypress Gardens that summer night when he thanked the voters who “indicted” him into the Florida Sports Hall of Fame and gave him a “standing observation.”

Pete was buddies with Don Coryell, a prominent branch of the Sid Gillman coaching tree. Gillman is the father of the modern vertical passing game, which Pete embraced when he recruited Steve Tensi and Fred Biletnikoff. FSU went from 5-foot-7 Eddie Feely to 6-foot-7 Steve Tensi at QB and Biletnikoff made catches that are still legendary. FSU offense elevated the former girls college into the ranks of major college football and Pete was its architect. FSU would play anybody, anywhere, anytime, a concept that Bobby Bowden used to turn the Seminoles into one of the four best programs in the country from 1987-2000.

Pete also had an eye for talent. Among his assistant coaches: Joe Gibbs, Bill Parcells, Don James, Bobby Bowden, Vince Gibson, Dan Henning and Ken Meyer.

What made Bill Peterson the most fun coach in America was his press conferences before and after games. Here are a few “Pete-isms” for you:

“You guys line up alphabetically by height.”

“You guys pair up in groups of three then line up in a circle.”

“Just remember the words of Henry Patrick: ‘Kill me or let me live.’”

“I’m the football coach here and don’t you remember it!”

“We can win this game if we just capitalize on our mistakes.”

“Lead us in a few words of silent prayer.”

“Men, I want you to stand on your helmets and put the sidelines under your arms.”

He really did say those things and they just rolled naturally off his tongue. Nobody in football entertained quite like Pete. He was my dear friend and this week I miss him more.

Published Nov. 23, 2026. Statistical update, Nov. 27: Florida lists Jadan Baugh at 980 rushing yards, 20 short of 1,000. Coaching references reflect the original publication date; Rick Stockstill is Florida State’s interim coach for today’s game.

A Florida player runs toward the end zone against Vanderbilt on Nov. 21 at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.

It’s Thanksgiving week, it’s Florida–Florida State week, and something besides the wishbone is liable to get broken.

Florida can win its eighth game Friday in Tallahassee. Florida State can win its sixth and go to a bowl. The Gators already have a bowl coming, but there’s a certain holiday pleasure in telling the relatives they can’t come along.

And FSU, win or lose Friday, already knows what's next — Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann was named its next head coach Monday night, though he'll stay with Georgia through the postseason.

Now, before somebody drags the good china out, I didn’t say we were back in the ’90s. Steve Spurrier and Bobby Bowden once went to Tallahassee ranked No. 1 and No. 2, then took the argument to New Orleans, where Florida won its first national championship. Back then you checked the polls after Florida–FSU. This year you check whether your cousin in Jacksonville has a spare bedroom.

Jacksonville, Tampa, Orlando? We can argue bowl geography after Friday. For now, the news is that this game matters again in both towns. And if you’re looking for somebody to throw a parade over seven wins, I wouldn’t ask Jon Sumrall to drive the float.

Seven wins and no gravy

I don’t ordinarily give a coach this much room to talk. Most of them can use up half a notebook saying they need to get better on third down. But Sumrall was asked Monday about winning seven games, and he gave a better answer than the question deserved.

“It’s better than six. It’s not as good as eight or nine or whatever. I’m so micro right now at the moment. I want to win every game we play. I also haven’t shied away from the fact that I think as we’re growing as a program, we’re trying to build the foundation. We can’t shy away from milestones that show growth, and that may mean the first winning conference record in several years since 2020. That’s a big deal.”

He went on to talk about how his team has responded after trailing at halftime and how many chances it has let get away. Then came the part I liked best:

“I probably am such a realist that I don’t really feel real excited about winning seven games. I also understand the good of that too, but I’m not like man, we’ve accomplished so much. I feel a little bit frustrated by some of the missed opportunities we’ve had. But we’ll get there. There’s been growth in this football team. It hasn’t maybe been as fast as I wanted at times, but there has been growth, and we still have areas where we have to grow a lot to get to where we want to go long term here.”

Want to hear him get considerably less diplomatic? Ask him why Jadan Baugh sometimes has to break a tackle just to get back to where he got the ball.

“It’s the offensive line’s job to make sure the running back gets back to line of scrimmage, and it’s the running back job to do something from there. We have at times not done a good enough job of getting the ball carrier back to line. That pisses me off. That drives me nuts.”

As for the times Aaron Philo hasn’t had enough pocket to get the ball downfield, Sumrall’s verdict applies there, too: “The O-line needs nobody to play well, for them to play well.”

You could put that on the wall in the offensive line room. I’d hang it at eye level.

Nineteen yards and a call to the Head Ball Coach

Saturday, Buster Faulkner put Philo and Baugh side by side in the shotgun against Vanderbilt. Philo sold the run to his left. Baugh took it off right tackle, planted his foot and cut through a crowd for the winning touchdown from 10 yards out. It was his 16th rushing touchdown of the season and a fine last impression to leave on the home crowd.

Now Baugh needs 19 yards at Doak to become the first Gator with back-to-back 1,000-yard rushing seasons. He got 1,170 last year, including 266 against these same Seminoles. You’d think a school that has handed the ball to Emmitt Smith, Errict Rhett and Fred Taylor would have checked that box by now. It hasn’t.

“Anytime you have the chance to be the first person to do something in a program like the University of Florida, that’s special,” Sumrall said Monday. “That’s unique.”

That sounded like something right out of the Head Ball Coach’s manual. Which is funny, because if anybody could have spared Baugh the trouble of being first, it was Steve Spurrier.

Rhett ran for 1,109 yards in 1991 and 1,289 in 1993. In between, he got 903 on 250 carries. Two hundred and fifty carries is not exactly neglect, even in an offense where the quarterback was liable to look downfield on the way to the water cooler. But there it was: 97 yards shy in 1992, and a school-record 4,163 for his career.

I brought that up with Spurrier on Monday. The Head Ball Coach told me, with some regret, that he wished he’d realized how close Rhett was. He would’ve given him the ball more.

Well, Jon, there’s your Thanksgiving advice from the man who gave us the Fun ’n’ Gun. Give the man the ball. The gravy can wait.

Published Nov. 23, 2026. Statistical update, Nov. 27: Florida lists Jadan Baugh at 980 rushing yards, 20 short of 1,000. Coaching references reflect the original publication date; Rick Stockstill is Florida State’s interim coach for today’s game.

Three Florida defenders celebrate during the Gators’ 34-27 win over Vanderbilt on Nov. 21 at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.

Long gone are the days when the renewal of the Florida-Florida State football rivalry had national championship implications but there is no lack of incentive for either the 20th-ranked Gators (7-4) or FSU (5-6) Friday afternoon (3:30 p.m., ABC) at Doak Campbell Stadium in Tallahassee.

Having already ensured only the second non-losing season since 2020, the Gators have their sights set on an eight-win regular season with the possibility of a ninth win in a bowl game. There was a time when nine wins was considered an off year for the Gators but since 2009, the Gators have had only five seasons with nine or more wins.

Just getting to eight wins in the regular season is a big deal for first year Florida coach Jon Sumrall since eight doubles up last year’s disaster in the fourth and final year of the Billy Napier era at UF. The Gators won eight in the regular season for Dan Mullen in 2020 and Napier got to eight with a Gasparilla Bowl win over Tulane in 2024.

The Gator Bowl (Jacksonville), ReliaQuest Bowl (Tampa) and Citrus Bowl (Orlando) all had their scouts at Florida’s 34-27 win over Vanderbilt. An eight-win Florida team would ensure a sellout crowd for any of those three games. Currently, the Gators are being projected as the host team against either Ohio State or Iowa in the ReliaQuest Bowl, while there are projections for Florida-Clemson in the Gator Bowl. The Citrus Bowl seems somewhat of a longshot but that could change based on the outcome of this weekend’s final games of the regular season.

Florida State isn’t lacking incentive. The Seminoles, who are 2-1 since Mike Norvell was fired, are one win away from bowl eligibility. Getting bowl eligible by beating arch-rival Florida will be a motivating factor in FSU’s preparation. Also, this game will be under close scrutiny for Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann, considered the No. 1 candidate to replace Norvell and the grandson of Jack Haskin, an assistant on Florida State’s first football team in 1947.

The Gators are listed as 4.5-point favorites to emerge as winners Friday.

RIVALRY WEEK IN THE SEC: WHAT’S AT STAKE (AP RANKINGS)

Georgia Tech (3-8) at No. 1 Georgia (10-1, 8-1 SEC): For Georgia Tech, this might be Brent Key’s last stand. Lose big and boosters might pull the plug. For Georgia, it’s a tuneup for the SEC Championship Game.

No. 5 Texas (9-2, 6-2 SEC) at Texas A&M (4-7, 1-7 SEC): For the Aggies and Mike Elko it’s a chance to salvage a nightmare season. The Aggies are the single most disappointing and overrated team in the country. Texas owns the tiebreaker with Tennessee and has more top tier wins than Alabama. Texas will be in the College Football Playoff.

Auburn (7-4, 5-4 SEC) at No. 6 Alabama (9-2, 5-2 SEC): Auburn has already ensured its first non-losing season since 2020. The Tigers haven’t beaten Alabama since the 2019 “Kick Six” game. There’s plenty at stake for Alabama. A loss to Auburn and the Tide probably won’t make the College Football Playoff. Even with a win, the Tide lost to Tennessee and doesn’t have the quality resume of Texas. Unless Texas and Tennessee lose Saturday, the best thing for Alabama is to avoid the SEC Championship Game. Right now, Auburn is projected to go either the Birmingham Bowl to face Minnesota or the Gator Bowl in Jacksonville to face Clemson.

No. 7 Tennessee (9-2, 6-2 SEC) at Vanderbilt (4-7, 1-7 SEC): Any Vanderbilt hope of a break even regular season and a bowl game was lost at Florida last weekend. To make the SEC Championship Game, the Vols need to beat Vandy and hope that Texas loses to the Aggies. The Vols beat Alabama so they own the tiebreaker. Tennessee is projected to make the College Football Playoff barring an upset at the hands of Vandy.

No. 19 Oklahoma (7-4, 5-3 SEC) at No. 24 Missouri (7-4, 4-4 SEC): The Sooners are trying to finish the season on a 4-game roll. They’re favored to get to the Citrus Bowl for a matchup with Iowa. Missouri tapped the brakes on a three loss in four game skid last week with a win over Kentucky. If the Tigers lose they’re probably going to the Liberty Bowl to face Cincinnati although there is a projection of a matchup with Baylor in the Texas Bowl.

Mississippi State (5-6, 2-6 SEC) at No. 23 Ole Miss (7-4, 4-4 SEC): An upset would make Mississippi State bowl eligible although it is possible that a 5-7 record could land a bowl invitation if there aren’t enough teams with winning records. In that case, CBS is predicting the Bulldogs and South Florida in the Gasparilla Bowl. Ole Miss is trying to finish out its once-promising season on a two-game win streak. An Ole Miss-Oklahoma State matchup is predicted for the Texas Bowl although there is another projection of an Indiana-Ole Miss Citrus Bowl.

No. 18 Louisville (8-3) at Kentucky (7-4, 5-4 SEC): Kentucky is shooting for an eighth regular season win, which would give first year head coach Will Stein a three-game improvement over the 2025 Wildcats who were coached by Mark Stoops. Pencil the Kentucky in for the winter home of the Wildcats, the Music City Bowl where it seems the opponent will be either Nebraska or Michigan. Louisville seems likely to go to the Pop Tarts Bowl in Orlando.

South Carolina (6-5, 4-5 SEC) at Clemson (7-4): Just a couple of weeks ago, the Gamecocks were dreaming of a 9-3 regular season. That was then, this is now, two losses later. Win or lose Saturday and it’s either the Birmingham Bowl or a ReliaQuest Bowl in Tampa against Ohio State. Clemson is hoping for a matchup with Auburn in the Gator Bowl.

LSU (6-5, 3-5 SEC) at Arkansas (4-7, 2-6 SEC): Those first year national championship dreams for LSU under Lane Kiffin died a long time ago. Now the goal is seven regular season wins. The Liberty Bowl wants to match LSU with Baylor but the Las Vegas Bowl is shooting for an LSU-Southern Cal matchup.

COUNTDOWN TO FIRING DAY: NOVEMBER 23, 2026 EDITION

EXTINCT SPECIES LIST

Mike Norvell, Florida State: Apparently, Florida State believes it can generate the funds necessary to hire Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann. Norvell is owed $48.7 million of which half is due this week, the other half paid in segments. The athletic department is nearly $500 million in debt.

Mike Locksley, Maryland: Charles Huff (Memphis) and former Notre Dame/LSU coach Brian Kelly are thought to be the leaders. Dan Mullen is on the wish list but he’s got a better situation at UNLV than being a perpetual bottom feeder in the Big Ten which is what the Maryland job is.

Dave Doeren, North Carolina State: Philip Rivers is the new head coach. The Wolfpack can be bowl eligible with a win Saturday over North Carolina.

Sonny Dykes, TCU: He was pink slipped Sunday. The Froggies are 5-6 with Texas Tech still on the schedule. There are enough oil gozillionaires tied to TCU to put up the cash to make a run at Lincoln Riley.

Dave Aranda, Baylor: Former Baylor Heisman winner Robert Griffin III wants the job but has no coaching experience. The smart hire would be UT-San Antonio’s Jeff Traylor.

Butch Jones, Arkansas State: It seems as if it’s Hugh Freeze’s job if he wants it, but there are folks who want Mike Norvell.

Phil Longo, Sam Houston: Josh McCown (QB coach Minnesota Vikings) is the one they would love to land. Former Sam Houston coach KC Keeler would love to come back after discovering the dead end street at Shirley Temple.

Scotty Walden, UTEP: They would love to land Florida Atlantic HBC Zach Kittley but he may have coached himself out of contention.

ON LIFE SUPPORT

Deion Sanders, Colorado: About the only thing saving Coach Prime is the $25.5 million it would take to fire him.

Brent Key, Georgia Tech: Tech is 3-8 and about to go belly up against Georgia in Athens. A growing segment of boosters want to hire Buster Faulkner.

Greg Schiano, Rutgers: He beat Penn State and he’s coming back next year, but his seat is going to be sizzling hot just the same.

Pat Narduzzi, Pittsburgh: They would love to move on to another coach, but they don’t have a spare $36 million to buy him out.

Joe Moorhead, Akron: Yeah, he’s on this list every year. He would already be off it if they had any money. They are just now realizing how good they had it when The Little Dweeb (Terry Bowden) was the HBC.

Tim Albin, Charlotte: He’s 2-20. They keep thinking he can do at Charlotte what he did at Ohio. Ain’t gonna happen.

ENDANGERED SPECIES LIST

Tony Elliott, Virginia: He’s won two straight and is now bowl eligible. He’s bought himself another year, but his seat will be very, very hot.

Bill O’Brien, Boston College: The Eagles are 5-6 but Miami’s next. If they’re smart – nobody is saying they are – they’ll keep him another year.

Lance Leipold, Kansas: KU is a basketball school that dabbles in football. Three straight losing seasons have the faithful thinking it’s time for a change.

Bill Belichick, North Carolina: If he beats NC State this weekend, he’ll be back another year. If not, all bets are off.

Dabo Swinney, Clemson: He really shouldn’t have a hot seat but boosters are mad because the Tigers haven’t won a national championship since 2018. He’s earned the right to leave on his own terms.

Ryan Day, Ohio State: The Buckeyes have lost four games this season, three since QB Julian Sayin went down with a season-ending injury. Why are boosters thinking about canning a coach with a career record of 89-16 with a national title?

items.title: Florida State Hires Georgia Defensive Coordinator Glenn Schumann as Head Coach
items.dek: Florida State hired Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann as its head football coach on Monday, four days before the Seminoles host Florida.
items.author: GatorBait Staff
items.html:
Glenn Schumann on the Georgia sideline in 2025. Photo by TarheelBornBred, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Florida State has hired Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann as its next head football coach, the school announced Monday, four days before the Seminoles host Florida in the regular-season finale.

Schumann, 36, agreed to a five-year contract, ESPN reported. He is expected to stay at Georgia through the College Football Playoff, according to ESPN. Georgia is 10-1 and ranked No. 1 in the latest Associated Press Top 25, according to ESPN.

It will be Schumann’s first job as a head coach. He joined Georgia’s staff in 2016 and was part of the Bulldogs’ national championship staffs in 2021 and 2022. Before that he worked at Alabama under Nick Saban, the Associated Press reported. 247Sports counted six national championship-winning staffs on his résumé.

“We are going to build a program that meets the championship expectation at Florida State,” Schumann said in a statement, as quoted by the AP. Athletics director Jeff Purinton called his abilities “elite” in the school’s statement.

The job is a family matter. Schumann’s grandfather, Jack Haskin, was an assistant coach on Florida State’s first football team in 1947, and his mother, Sherry Schumann, earned her bachelor’s and master’s degrees at the school, according to the school’s statement.

Florida State opened the search after firing Mike Norvell in early November, following consecutive Atlantic Coast Conference losses to Louisville, Miami and Clemson, the AP reported. The Seminoles are 5-6 and need a win Friday to reach bowl eligibility, according to ESPN.

Florida (7-4) is No. 20 in the AP poll, according to ESPN, and plays at Doak Campbell Stadium on Friday at 3:30 p.m. ET on ABC.

The new coach is familiar to the Gators’ staff. Florida offensive coordinator Buster Faulkner worked with Schumann at Georgia, and the AP quoted Faulkner as saying, “He knows what winning looks like.”

This story is based on reports by the Associated Press, ESPN and 247Sports and on Florida State’s statement.

items.title: Fourth and The Game
items.dek: Jadan Baugh will be the focal point of today's game at Tallahassee. His quest to be the first Florida Gator running back to have back-to-back 1000-yard rushing seasons is a great talking point for the broadcast.
items.author: Eddie Gilley
items.html:
Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.

Jadan Baugh will be the focal point of today’s game at Tallahassee. His quest to be the first Florida Gator running back to have back-to-back 1000-yard rushing seasons is a great talking point for the broadcast. It is also a critical issue for Gator fans for another reason. The Gators will need Baugh to have another big day against the Noles for them to leave Doak with a win.

Can Buster Faulkner scheme up a run game that will give him a chance to break some big plays, or will he insist on running him up the middle for a few yards a carry? Baugh gained most of his yards last week when he was able to get to the edge of the defense. Everyone has seen the still shot of the entire Vandy defense in the backfield before Jadan even got the ball. He still turned that play into a first down run. Jadan Baugh has proven he is a great back. And he has done that without a great offensive line. They have been good at times but with a great line, he would be looking at 1500 yards for the season.

The passing game will have to be efficient to provide some relief to the running game. Philo had a decent game last week. He just needs another decent one this week. He needs to be the game manager not the game changer. That is difficult for most quarterbacks. He has the talent to lead this team through the air, but he doesn’t have the protection to be able to drop back and go through three options. He’s proven that he can win on the road in the SEC. The crowd at Doak may not be as vocal as usual, but the band will still be loud! Maintaining his composure will be key in a heated, rivalry game. Take the easy throws, don’t turn the ball over and give the Gators a chance to win the game with your feet.

The defense just needs to make the handful of plays to make crucial stops. Last week the game was too close because they didn’t make the plays. The coaches had them in the right positions, but the players didn’t execute. The touchdown right before the half should have been an interception. The final drive could have ended twice before it got critical. Several times there were Gators unblocked that failed to make the tackle in the backfield. Fix those mistakes and the crowd will be mostly Gators by the start of the fourth quarter. Continue to make them and the Gators will be in a street fight to the very end. The defense has played well enough to win the last six games. They need one more great effort, especially up front to pressure the FSU QB and keep him in the pocket.

Rivalry games are full of emotion. The first half is played on emotion, and the second half is won with talent and effort. The Gators are the most talented team. FSU will have an early emotional edge. The crowd will be in the game early. The Gators have started poorly most of the season. The Gators need to find a way to do something different today. Start the game on fire! Come out of the tunnel with their hair on fire. Match the intensity of Coach Sumrall. Shut the crowd up early and win this one going away at the finish. Time will tell if the Gators can do just that!

feature.title: Behind the Sticks: Florida at Florida State
feature.dek: The line moved from 5.5 to 6.5, the total never budged, and Jadan Baugh needs 20 yards to make Florida history. Behind the Sticks breaks down Florida at Florida State by the numbers.
feature.author: Brenden Martin
feature.html:
Illustration: GatorBait Media (AI-assisted)

The line moved. That is the first thing to know about Friday.

Florida opened as a 5.5-point favorite in Tallahassee. By Thursday night the number was 6.5 at nearly every book, and the moneyline sat around minus-235. Lines do not move a full point in a rivalry week by accident. They move because the people who bet for a living looked at the same two teams you are looking at and decided the gap is wider than the first number said.

The total tells its own story. It opened at 53.5 and it has not budged. The market expects points. It just expects more of them from one side.

And then there is the smallest number of the week. Twenty. Jadan Baugh has 980 rushing yards. Twenty more on Friday and he reaches 1,000 for the second straight season, something no Florida running back has ever done. Not Emmitt Smith. Not Fred Taylor. Not anybody who has ever worn the uniform.

Here is what the free part of this column will tell you. Florida is 7-4 and ranked 20th. Florida State is 5-6 and playing for its bowl life in front of its own crowd. The series stands at 39-28-2, Florida has won the last two, and Baugh ran for 266 yards on this defense a year ago. Florida State also has a new head coach coming, Glenn Schumann, and he will not be on that sideline Friday. Interim coach Rick Stockstill runs the Seminoles, which means Florida is walking into a stadium where the home team is playing for its season with a coach who is keeping the seat warm.

What the free part will not tell you is where this game is actually won. That part is in the matchup numbers, and one of them is so lopsided it explains the line move all by itself. There is also one number that cuts the other way, and it is the reason this game is not the lock the crowd thinks it is. Both of them are below. That is the deal here. The tease is free. The truth costs an email address.

Start with the run game, because the whole game starts there.

Florida rushes for 169.5 yards a game. Florida State allows 171.0 rushing yards a game. That run defense ranks 101st in the country, and it gives up 4.55 yards a carry. Last week an ordinary NC State rushing attack ran for 172 yards on the Seminoles. Baugh is not ordinary, and he does not need 266 again. He needs his season average and a defense that has spent eleven games proving it cannot hold the line of scrimmage.

Third down is the quieter edge. Florida converts 45.9 percent of its third downs, 24th in the country. Florida State's defense gets off the field 58.1 percent of the time, which is another way of saying it allows 41.9 percent, 107th nationally. Drives that should die keep living. Against a run defense this soft, long drives are not a hope. They are the arithmetic.

Now the number that cuts the other way, because this column tells the truth or it is worthless.

Florida's red-zone defense is a problem. It ranks 107th in the country, allowing scores on 88.6 percent of trips inside the 20. Florida State's red-zone offense ranks 40th. The Gators have also allowed at least 23 points in eight of their last nine games, and they give up 26.3 a game on the season. That is why the total sits at 53.5 and why nobody sharp is treating the under as free money. Florida can control this game on the ground and still give up points in bunches when drives reach the red zone. Both things are true at the same time.

Vernell Brown III being out matters here too. His knee surgery ends his season, and without him Florida's passing game loses the player who stretched defenses away from Baugh. Florida averages 226.1 passing yards a game for the season. The honest read is that his absence pushes even more of Friday onto the ground game, which happens to be the one place Florida State cannot stand up. Sometimes the injury report and the matchup point the same direction. This is one of those times.

So here is the picture the numbers paint, without any orange and blue on it. Florida covers 6.5 if Baugh gets a full workload, because Florida State has not stopped a real rushing attack all season and third down tilts the field for four quarters. Florida State stays inside the number if it turns red-zone trips into touchdowns the way the season says it can, and if the crowd and the bowl stakes buy it two short fields.

The line moved a full point for a reason. Behind the sticks, the reason is 169.5 against 171.0, and a running back who needs 20 yards to make history against the defense least built to stop him from getting them.

Friday at 3:30. The numbers have said their piece. Now the game gets its turn.

See you in Tallahassee.
